passage: I'm Mahima, and I sit two benches behind Deepak, so I saw what happened after the results. Deepak got the top marks in maths and science, and the group by the water cooler went quiet when Deepak walked up. Someone muttered "teacher's pet". Deepak didn't argue. Next day Deepak still put the chapter summaries on the bench, saying "take them if they help", and never mentioned the marks. Nobody said thanks. I can't tell what Deepak felt; maybe hurt, maybe fine. But Deepak's next test was just as strong, and by Friday two of them were copying the summaries. Nobody was really friendly yet. Deepak just kept sitting at the same bench.

qa.q: Where does Mahima sit compared with Deepak?
qa.a: Mahima sits two benches behind Deepak.

qa.q: What might Deepak have felt when the group went quiet, and why is Mahima unsure?
qa.a: Deepak may have felt hurt, or may have been fine; Mahima is unsure because Deepak did not argue or say anything about it.

qa.q: What could Deepak do if the coldness carries on?
qa.a: Stay warm and keep sharing notes without flaunting marks, keep working at the same level, and accept that some distance may pass. 🙂

qa.q: How might the group by the water cooler see Deepak's summaries?
qa.a: Probably with mixed feelings: perhaps stung by the marks, yet the summaries are useful, since two of them ended up copying them.

grounding: Friends grow cold after Deepak scores well, and Deepak stays warm, shares notes and keeps the effort up, as seen by a classmate.

passage: In the corridor outside the staffroom, Omkar held the maths answer sheet face down so nobody could see the red 34. Shame ran hot up the neck. Papa had told the whole family about the tuition fees, and now this. I'm a waste, Omkar thought, and sat on the stairs. Then Tushar Sir came out with a stack of copybooks. "Come in, if you want." Omkar almost said no. Instead, Omkar took a pen and wrote: "Ran out of time on Q5. Guessed the geometry. Slept four hours." "Is that you, or one paper?" Tushar Sir asked. Omkar looked at the list for a while. "One paper." "Good. Let's plan the next one."

qa.q: What did Omkar write on the list?
qa.a: Omkar wrote: "Ran out of time on Q5. Guessed the geometry. Slept four hours."

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling on the stairs, and what thought showed it?
qa.a: Omkar felt ashamed, and the thought "I'm a waste" and the worry about Papa telling the family about the tuition fees show it.

qa.q: Which choice helped Omkar, and why?
qa.a: Omkar accepted the invitation and wrote down what went wrong, which separated one paper from Omkar's worth and opened the way to a plan.

qa.q: How does Tushar Sir see Omkar's result?
qa.a: As one paper, not the whole student; the question "Is that you, or one paper?" and the offer to plan the next one show it.

grounding: One low result leaves Omkar feeling worthless; Omkar lists what went wrong and a teacher offers a recovery plan.

passage: On Monday the coaching centre's corridor board went up again: names in batches, A at the top, D at the bottom, and Devika's name in D. The announcement came fast: "D batch, you still have time, but the crash course closes Friday." Devika's chest tightened all evening, and the pile of notes looked like a wall. At dinner Devika pushed rice around the plate. Manjula Mausi, visiting from Pune, asked what was wrong. "They keep saying D batch like it's an illness," Devika said. "And then the crash course pops up." Devika stopped. "They need us scared." Mausi said nothing, only nodded. Next morning Devika wrote a plan at a steady pace and said Papa would see it too.

qa.q: Which batch was Devika's name in on the corridor board?
qa.a: Devika's name was in D, the bottom batch.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling on the evening after the board went up, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Devika felt anxious and small; the tightened chest, the wall of notes and the pushed-around rice show it.

qa.q: What small step would help Devika if the fear comes back?
qa.a: Keep to the steady plan, remember the board is part of how the centre sells its crash course, and talk to Manjula Mausi or Papa if Devika starts to crumble.

qa.q: How might the coaching centre see the ranking board?
qa.a: As a way to sell fear and the crash course to families; Devika's remark that the crash course pops up right after the batches points that way.

grounding: A coaching centre ranks students in batches and sells the crash course; Devika notices this and goes at own pace with adult support.

passage:
Counsellor's note. Tushar came to my room at lunch. Tushar said Omkar has stopped bringing a tiffin, is barely sleeping before boards, and said yesterday, "What's the point of all this." Others in the group had laughed it off. Tushar did not. Tushar sat with Omkar on the ground steps, suggested a short walk instead of more revision, and then said to me, "I'm telling you because I'm worried, not because I'm betraying anyone." I thanked Tushar. That afternoon I met Omkar, and with Omkar's knowledge I phoned Omkar's parents. We will check in again next week.
- Ms. Iyer, school counsellor

qa.q: Where did Tushar sit with Omkar?
qa.a: Tushar sat with Omkar on the ground steps.

qa.q: What was Tushar worried about, and what showed it?
qa.a: Tushar was worried that Omkar felt low and hopeless; Omkar had stopped bringing a tiffin, was barely sleeping and said "What's the point of all this", and Tushar did not laugh it off. 🤍

qa.q: How could Tushar keep supporting Omkar after telling the counsellor?
qa.a: Keep sitting with Omkar, offer breaks and walks, stay kind, and let the adults who now know help.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel about Tushar telling Ms. Iyer?
qa.a: Possibly exposed or uneasy at first, but also noticed and looked after; Tushar's words that this was worry and not betrayal may help.

grounding: A friend sees Omkar stop eating and sleeping before boards, sits with Omkar, offers a break and tells a counsellor.

passage:
Dear Preeti,
You asked how the physics paper went. Badly. Two whole questions blank, and I walked out with my ears burning. My first thought was the old one: "You're useless, no phone, no sleep until you're perfect." Then I pictured you handing me that same paper, and I knew what I'd say to you: "That hurt. It's one paper. What shall we fix?" So I said it to myself. I wrote down the two topics I skipped, booked a doubt session with Mr Rao for Thursday, and went to sleep. I still want a good score. It's just easier to work when I'm not my own enemy. 🙂 Write back with your chemistry news!
Jagdish

qa.q: How many questions did Jagdish leave blank?
qa.a: Jagdish left two whole questions blank.

qa.q: What did Jagdish realise by picturing Preeti handing over the same paper?
qa.a: That Jagdish would speak kindly to a friend, saying "It's one paper. What shall we fix?", and could speak to oneself in the same way.

qa.q: What small steps did Jagdish take next, and why do they help?
qa.a: Jagdish wrote down the two skipped topics, booked a doubt session with Mr Rao and slept; these are concrete, so the plan replaces punishment. 🙂

qa.q: How might Preeti feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Probably trusted and maybe reassured, since Jagdish shares a bad result openly and then asks about Preeti's chemistry news.

grounding: After a bad paper Jagdish speaks to self as to a friend and plans the next one without lowering standards.

passage: The corridor had emptied, but Madhuri Ma'am was still at the board with a marker. Vandana hovered at the door, cheeks warm. "I didn't get the integration steps," Vandana said. "I didn't want to ask in class." "Come, sit." Ma'am redrew the graph slowly and waited each time Vandana frowned. The tea on her desk went cold. Vandana felt thankful, and a little small for needing this. "Thank you, Ma'am. I know you have to go home." "Bring me whatever you get stuck on." Vandana walked out with the notebook still open, already starting the first sum.

qa.q: What had Vandana not understood?
qa.a: Vandana had not understood the integration steps.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling about needing help, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Thankful but a little embarrassed; the warm cheeks, the hovering at the door and the earlier reluctance to ask in class show it. 😊

qa.q: How could Vandana use the extra time well?
qa.a: Bring whatever Vandana gets stuck on, and practise sums soon after, as Vandana began doing on the way out.

qa.q: How might Madhuri Ma'am see a student who stays back to ask?
qa.a: As someone willing to learn; Ma'am stayed while the tea went cold and invited more questions.

grounding: A teacher stays after class to explain what Vandana missed; Vandana feels thankful and a little embarrassed and uses the time.

passage: Wei printed three pages before dinner in Vancouver: graduate figures from a design school, the starting pay listed on its site, and a plan. Wei's mother, Xin, expected engineering, like Wei's uncle. "I know you worry about jobs," Wei began, hands not quite steady. "Here is the share of last year's design graduates who were in work. And here is a course at the same university that mixes engineering and design, if you'd rather have both." Xin scanned the pages in silence. "One term," Wei said. "Let me take the design elective and keep science. If my science marks drop, we talk again." Xin folded her reading glasses. "Show me the elective's timetable," she said at last.

qa.q: What three things did Wei print before dinner?
qa.a: Wei printed graduate figures from a design school, the starting pay listed on its site, and a plan.

qa.q: What is Wei feeling as the talk begins, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Wei is nervous but determined; the hands not quite steady and the careful preparation show it.

qa.q: Which part of Wei's approach makes agreement easier, and why?
qa.a: The one-term trial with science kept: it is small and can be undone, so Xin risks little.

qa.q: What might Xin be worried about?
qa.a: Wei's job prospects, since Xin expected engineering like Wei's uncle; asking for the timetable shows Xin is taking the plan seriously.

grounding: Wei wants design while the family expects engineering, and presents real paths, numbers and a trial term.

passage:
Ujjwal put down his tea. "Parveen, the form is filled. Science with maths."
"Papa, may I ask why you chose it without asking me?"
"Because it is the best path. Look at Bhavesh, my cousin's boy. Big job, big flat."
"I'm happy for Bhavesh, Papa. But I like history and writing."
"History gives you what?"
"That's what I'd like to ask someone who knows. Can we meet the school counsellor together? I'll listen to the facts. I'm not saying no to you. I'm saying I have a mind."
Ujjwal was quiet for a moment. "Counsellor. Fine. Saturday. But you listen to me too."
"Always, Papa."

qa.q: Who does Ujjwal hold up as an example?
qa.a: Ujjwal holds up Bhavesh, his cousin's boy, who has a big job.

qa.q: What is Parveen wanting in this talk, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Parveen wants a say and reasons without a quarrel; asking politely, offering to listen to the facts and saying "I have a mind" show it.

qa.q: What could Parveen do if the Saturday meeting does not change Ujjwal's mind?
qa.a: Keep asking respectfully for the reasons, perhaps bring another trusted elder as a bridge, and keep showing Ujjwal that listening goes both ways. ❤️

qa.q: Why might Ujjwal push the science stream so firmly?
qa.a: Ujjwal sees Bhavesh's big job as a safe future and probably wants that security for Parveen, which is why the choice came before the conversation.

grounding: A stream is being decided by a relative's success; Parveen stays respectful, asks for reasons and proposes a counsellor as a bridge.

passage:
Counsellor's note. Ganga came to see me after the parent-teacher meeting. Ganga's mother works long shifts in a canteen and Ganga's father drives an auto; both want Ganga in the science stream "so the sacrifice counts". Ganga said, "They have given up so much. How can I say I want to study design? It feels like I owe them my whole future." Ganga's eyes were wet, yet Ganga thanked me twice and said the sacrifice is real. I suggested telling the parents, kindly, what interests Ganga, and thanking them in the same conversation. Ganga wrote three sentences and rehearsed them. I will sit in if Ganga wants.
- Farhan, school counsellor

qa.q: What work does Ganga's father do?
qa.a: Ganga's father drives an auto.

qa.q: What is Ganga feeling toward the parents, and how do both sides show?
qa.a: Ganga feels indebted and trapped: Ganga says they have given up so much and "I owe them my whole future", yet wants to study design.

qa.q: What did Farhan suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To tell the parents kindly what interests Ganga while thanking them in the same conversation, since gratitude does not have to erase Ganga's own choices.

qa.q: How might Ganga's parents feel on hearing this?
qa.a: Perhaps surprised or worried about the future, but also moved by the thanks; they want the sacrifice to count.

grounding: Ganga feels both indebted and trapped by the parents' sacrifice and is helped to honour it while stating an honest interest.

passage:
Class teacher's note on stream forms. Hansa handed in the commerce form on the same day as Arohi and four others. When I asked why, Hansa said, "We've always done everything together, so it's easier." Earlier Hansa had told me quietly that biology interests Hansa more than accounts. Arohi told me separately that Arohi would have been happy for Hansa to choose differently. I did not push. I asked Hansa to write two lines on what Hansa wants from each stream and to keep the form for a night. I also said that timetables change friendships whichever stream anyone picks. Hansa took the form home.
- Class teacher

qa.q: Which stream's form did Hansa hand in?
qa.a: Hansa handed in the commerce form.

qa.q: What does Hansa's remark about doing everything together suggest about Hansa's motive?
qa.a: That Hansa wants to stay with the group and avoid being left out, even though biology interests Hansa more.

qa.q: What would you advise Hansa to do with the form?
qa.a: Write down what Hansa wants from each stream and choose from that, remembering that friendships change anyway, so no one can be blamed for it later.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Hansa's choice?
qa.a: Arohi said privately that Arohi would have been happy for Hansa to choose differently, so Arohi may not have expected Hansa to follow for the group's sake.

grounding: Hansa follows the group into one stream to stay together; the teacher's note shows a different private interest and a nudge to choose independently.
